questions.stem: The correct order of acidity for the following compounds is
questions.solution: An ortho-OH stabilises the carboxylate by intramolecular hydrogen bonding, which strongly raises acidity. 2,6-Dihydroxybenzoic acid (I) has two such hydrogen bonds and is the strongest, ahead of salicylic acid (II) with one. With OH at the meta position (III) only its electron-withdrawing inductive effect acts, so the acid is slightly stronger than benzoic acid. At the para position (IV) the +R donation of OH dominates and weakens the acid, which gives I > II > III > IV.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; matches the official key printed in the paper (A)

questions.stem:
The major product of the following reaction sequence is
Starting ketone —i) HCHO (excess)/NaOH, heat ii) HCHO/H⁺ (catalytic amount)→ ?
questions.solution: The ketone has a single α-hydrogen, so with base it undergoes one crossed aldol addition to HCHO, giving PhCOC(CH₃)₂CH₂OH. Excess formaldehyde in hot alkali then acts as a hydride donor (a crossed Cannizzaro-type reduction) and reduces the C=O to CH–OH, giving the 1,3-diol PhCH(OH)C(CH₃)₂CH₂OH. With HCHO and a trace of acid, this 1,3-diol forms a cyclic formal, 5,5-dimethyl-4-phenyl-1,3-dioxane.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; matches the official key printed in the paper (A)

questions.stem:
For 'invert sugar', the correct statement(s) is(are)
(Given: specific rotations of (+)-sucrose, (+)-maltose, L-(−)-glucose and L-(+)-fructose in aqueous solution are +66°, +140°, −52° and +92°, respectively)

options.text: 'invert sugar' is prepared by acid catalyzed hydrolysis of maltose
'invert sugar' is an equimolar mixture of D-(+)-glucose and D-(−)-fructose
on reaction with Br₂ water, 'invert sugar' forms saccharic acid as one of the products

questions.solution: Invert sugar comes from hydrolysing sucrose, not maltose, and is an equimolar mixture of D-glucose and D-fructose. The D enantiomers have rotations opposite to the given L values: D-glucose +52° and D-fructose −92°. For a 1:1 mixture the rotation is (52 − 92)/2 = −20°, which is where the change in sign from sucrose (+66°) comes from. Bromine water is a mild oxidant that turns glucose into gluconic acid; making saccharic (glucaric) acid needs HNO₃.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; matches the official key printed in the paper (B, C)

questions.stem: Reagent(s) which can be used to bring about the following transformation is(are)
questions.solution: Only the aldehyde must be reduced to CH₂OH, while the carboxylic acid, the tert-butyl ester and the epoxide survive. NaBH₄ in ethanol reduces aldehydes quickly and leaves acids, esters and epoxides intact. Raney Ni/H₂ under mild conditions also reduces the C=O of the aldehyde selectively. LiAlH₄ would also reduce the acid and the ester and could open the epoxide. BH₃ reduces carboxylic acids very fast, so it would attack the COOH.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; matches the official key printed in the paper (C, D)

questions.stem:
Among the following, reaction(s) which gives(give) tert-butyl benzene as the major product is(are)
(A) benzene + (CH₃)₃CBr, NaOC₂H₅
(B) benzene + (CH₃)₂CHCH₂Cl, AlCl₃
(C) benzene + (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, H₂SO₄
(D) benzene + (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH, BF₃·OEt₂
questions.solution: Friedel–Crafts alkylation needs an acid that makes a carbocation. NaOEt is a base, so with tert-butyl bromide it only causes E2 elimination to isobutylene, and benzene does not react. AlCl₃ with isobutyl chloride, and BF₃ with isobutyl alcohol, both give a primary cation (or cation-like complex) that undergoes a hydride shift to the tert-butyl cation. Protonating isobutylene with H₂SO₄ gives the tert-butyl cation directly. In each of these three cases the cation alkylates benzene to give tert-butylbenzene.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; matches the official key printed in the paper (B, C, D)

questions.passage: Treatment of compound O with KMnO₄/H⁺ gave P, which on heating with ammonia gave Q. The compound Q on treatment with Br₂/NaOH produced R. On strong heating, Q gave S, which on further treatment with ethyl 2-bromopropanoate in the presence of KOH followed by acidification, gave a compound T.
questions.solution: Hot acidic KMnO₄ oxidises both benzylic side chains to COOH, giving phthalic acid (P). Heating it with ammonia gives phthalamide (Q), and strong heating of Q loses NH₃ to give phthalimide (S). Br₂/NaOH carries out a Hofmann bromamide degradation on both CONH₂ groups of phthalamide. Each amide loses one carbon and becomes NH₂, so R is benzene-1,2-diamine.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; matches the official key printed in the paper (A)

questions.passage: Treatment of compound O with KMnO₄/H⁺ gave P, which on heating with ammonia gave Q. The compound Q on treatment with Br₂/NaOH produced R. On strong heating, Q gave S, which on further treatment with ethyl 2-bromopropanoate in the presence of KOH followed by acidification, gave a compound T.
questions.solution: S is phthalimide. KOH deprotonates its N–H, and the imide anion displaces bromide from ethyl 2-bromopropanoate (Gabriel synthesis), giving N-phthalimido ethyl propanoate. Hydrolysis and acidification release the phthalic acid part and the ester, leaving CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH. So T is alanine.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; matches the official key printed in the paper (B)
